summary.text: For any proper odd prime divisor \(p\mid n\), the factors \(2^k-1\) with \(k\) a multiple of \(p-1\) supply enough powers of \(p\) to show \(p\mid a(n-1)\), contradicting the hypothesis; the remaining composite possibility, a power of \(2\), is excluded using \(v_2((2^k)!)=2^k-1\) and the oddness of \(\prod_{j=1}^{n-2}(2^j-1)\). Once \(n\) is prime, any exponent \(0<\ell<n-1\) with \(2^\ell\equiv1\pmod n\) makes \(n\) divide a factor of the product and hence \(a(n-1)\), so the hypothesis would force \(n\mid2^{n-2}\), an impossibility; therefore the order of \(2\) is \(n-1\).

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
P(m):=\prod_{j=1}^{m-1}(2^j-1),\qquad
B(m):=2^{m-1}P(m).
\]
Thus, for every positive integer \(m\), the sequence term is
\[
a(m)=\frac{B(m)}{m!}.
\]
We first establish that this quotient is indeed an integer and record the divisibility information that will be needed later.

For a prime \(p\) and a positive integer \(N\), write \(v_p(N)\) for the exponent of \(p\) in \(N\). We use the standard factorial estimate
\[
 (p-1)v_p(m!)<m \qquad(m>0). \tag{1}
\]
For example, this follows immediately from Legendre's formula
\[
v_p(m!)=\sum_{i\geq 1}\left\lfloor\frac m{p^i}\right\rfloor:
\]
the finite sum on the right is strictly less than the infinite geometric sum
\(\sum_{i\geq1}m/p^i=m/(p-1)\).

We will also repeatedly use Fermat's congruence. If \(p\) is an odd prime, then
\[
2^{p-1}\equiv1\pmod p,
\]
and hence, for every positive integer \(s\),
\[
p\mid 2^{(p-1)s}-1. \tag{2}
\]
Consequently, if
\[
(p-1)t<m,
\]
then the \(t\) distinct positive indices
\[
p-1,\ 2(p-1),\ldots,\ t(p-1)
\]
all lie between \(1\) and \(m-1\). By (2), each of the corresponding factors in \(P(m)\) is divisible by \(p\). Therefore
\[
p^t\mid P(m). \tag{3}
\]

We can now prove the integrality of \(a(m)\). Let \(p^e\) be any prime power dividing \(m!\), so that \(e\leq v_p(m!)\).

If \(p=2\), (1) gives \(e\leq v_2(m!)<m\), hence \(e\leq m-1\). Thus \(2^e\) divides the factor \(2^{m-1}\) in \(B(m)\).

If \(p\) is odd, then
\[
(p-1)e\leq(p-1)v_p(m!)<m.
\]
Taking \(t=e\) in (3), we obtain \(p^e\mid P(m)\), and hence \(p^e\mid B(m)\).

Every prime power occurring in \(m!\) therefore divides \(B(m)\), with the required multiplicity. It follows that
\[
m!\mid B(m).
\]
Thus \(a(m)=B(m)/m!\) is an integer, and we have the exact identity
\[
a(m)m!=B(m)=2^{m-1}P(m). \tag{4}
\]
Moreover, exact division gives, for every prime \(p\),
\[
v_p(a(m))=v_p(B(m))-v_p(m!). \tag{5}
\]

We next prove the key lemma concerning a proper odd prime divisor of \(n\).

**Lemma.** Suppose \(n>2\), \(p\) is an odd prime, \(p\mid n\), and \(p\neq n\). Then
\[
p\mid a(n-1). \tag{6}
\]

Write \(n=pq\). Since \(p\neq n\) and \(n>0\), the quotient \(q\) is not \(1\); it is also not \(0\). Hence \(q\geq2\). Put
\[
x=q-1>0.
\]
Then
\[
n-1=pq-1=px+(p-1). \tag{7}
\]
Because the integers \(px+1,\ldots,px+p-1\) are not divisible by \(p\), adjoining these factors to \((px)!\) does not change its \(p\)-adic valuation. Therefore
\[
v_p((n-1)!)=v_p((px)!). \tag{8}
\]
Among the factors of \((px)!\), the multiples of \(p\) are
\(p,2p,\ldots,xp\). Removing one factor \(p\) from each of them leaves the factors of \(x!\). Hence
\[
v_p((px)!)=x+v_p(x!). \tag{9}
\]
Let
\[
v:=v_p((n-1)!).
\]
By (8) and (9), \(v=x+v_p(x!)\). Using (1) for the positive integer \(x\), we have
\[
(p-1)v_p(x!)<x.
\]
It follows that
\[
\begin{aligned}
(p-1)(v+1)
 &= (p-1)\bigl(x+v_p(x!)+1\bigr)\\
 &= (p-1)x+(p-1)+(p-1)v_p(x!)\\
 &< (p-1)x+(p-1)+x\\
 &=px+(p-1)\\
 &=n-1,
\end{aligned} \tag{10}
\]
where the last equality is (7).

Apply (3) with \(m=n-1\) and \(t=v+1\). Inequality (10) gives
\[
p^{v+1}\mid P(n-1),
\]
and hence also
\[
p^{v+1}\mid B(n-1).
\]
Thus \(v_p(B(n-1))\geq v+1\). Since \(v=v_p((n-1)!)\), equation (5) yields
\[
v_p(a(n-1))\geq1.
\]
This proves (6).

We now exclude the case that \(n\) is a power of \(2\). Suppose
\[
n=2^k>2
\]
and, contrary to what we want to prove, suppose
\[
n\mid a(n-1)+2^{n-2}. \tag{11}
\]
Multiplying (11) by \((n-1)!\), and using \(n(n-1)!=n!\), gives
\[
n!\mid a(n-1)(n-1)!+2^{n-2}(n-1)!.
\]
By (4),
\[
a(n-1)(n-1)!=B(n-1)=2^{n-2}P(n-1).
\]
Consequently,
\[
n!\mid 2^{n-2}\bigl(P(n-1)+(n-1)!\bigr). \tag{12}
\]

For a power of two, Legendre's formula gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
v_2((2^k)!)
 &=\sum_{i=1}^{k}\left\lfloor\frac{2^k}{2^i}\right\rfloor\\
 &=2^{k-1}+2^{k-2}+\cdots+1\\
 &=2^k-1.
\end{aligned}
\]
Thus, because \(n=2^k\),
\[
v_2(n!)=n-1,
\]
so \(2^{n-1}\mid n!\). From (12) we obtain
\[
2^{n-1}\mid2^{n-2}\bigl(P(n-1)+(n-1)!\bigr).
\]
Cancelling the positive factor \(2^{n-2}\), we find
\[
2\mid P(n-1)+(n-1)!. \tag{13}
\]
Since \(n>2\), the factorial \((n-1)!\) is even. Equation (13) would therefore imply that \(P(n-1)\) is even. But every factor \(2^j-1\) in \(P(n-1)\) is odd, so their product is odd. This contradiction proves that no power of \(2\) greater than \(2\) can satisfy (11).

We now prove that any \(n>2\) satisfying the conjectured divisibility is prime. Assume
\[
n\mid a(n-1)+2^{n-2}. \tag{14}
\]
Every positive integer is either a power of \(2\), or has an odd prime divisor: after removing all factors of \(2\), if anything greater than \(1\) remains, choose a prime divisor of the remaining odd number. The power-of-two possibility has just been excluded. Hence \(n\) has an odd prime divisor \(p\).

If \(p=n\), then \(n\) itself is prime and we are done. Suppose instead that \(p\neq n\). The lemma then gives
\[
p\mid a(n-1).
\]
Also \(p\mid n\), so (14) implies
\[
p\mid a(n-1)+2^{n-2}.
\]
Subtracting the divisibility by \(a(n-1)\), we obtain
\[
p\mid2^{n-2}.
\]
Since \(p\) is prime, this would force \(p\mid2\), hence \(p=2\), contrary to the fact that \(p\) is odd. Thus the alternative \(p\neq n\) is impossible, and necessarily \(p=n\). Therefore \(n\) is prime.

It remains to prove that \(2\) is a primitive root modulo this prime \(n\). Since \(n>2\), it is an odd prime, so \(2\not\equiv0\pmod n\). Fermat's theorem gives
\[
2^{n-1}\equiv1\pmod n. \tag{15}
\]
We claim that there is no positive exponent \(\ell<n-1\) for which
\[
2^\ell\equiv1\pmod n. \tag{16}
\]
Indeed, suppose such an \(\ell\) existed. Then
\[
n\mid2^\ell-1.
\]
Because \(1\leq\ell<n-1\), the number \(2^\ell-1\) is one of the factors in
\[
P(n-1)=\prod_{j=1}^{n-2}(2^j-1).
\]
It follows that
\[
n\mid P(n-1),
\]
and therefore \(n\mid B(n-1)\). By (4), this says
\[
n\mid a(n-1)(n-1)!. \tag{17}
\]
None of \(1,2,\ldots,n-1\) is divisible by the prime \(n\), so
\[
\gcd\bigl(n,(n-1)!\bigr)=1.
\]
Euclid's lemma applied to (17) consequently gives
\[
n\mid a(n-1). \tag{18}
\]
Combining (18) with the original assumption (14), we obtain
\[
n\mid2^{n-2}.
\]
A prime dividing a power of \(2\) must divide \(2\), which would imply \(n=2\). This contradicts \(n>2\). Hence no \(\ell\) satisfying \(0<\ell<n-1\) can satisfy (16).

By (15), the multiplicative order of \(2\) modulo \(n\) divides, and is at most, \(n-1\); the preceding paragraph shows that no smaller positive exponent gives \(1\). Thus the order is exactly \(n-1\). Finally, because \(n\) is prime,
\[
\varphi(n)=n-1.
\]
Therefore \(2\) has multiplicative order \(\varphi(n)\) modulo \(n\), which is precisely to say that \(2\) is a primitive root modulo \(n\).

We have proved that every integer \(n>2\) satisfying
\[
n\mid a(n-1)+2^{n-2}
\]
is prime and has \(2\) as a primitive root modulo \(n\), as claimed.
